steps.prompt: Same two facts, different joining words. How does the meaning change?
steps.a: It was raining, so we played outside.
steps.b: It was raining, but we played outside.
steps.reveal: “So” says the rain caused the outdoor play, which makes no sense. “But” shows a surprise: we played despite the rain. In a compound sentence, the joining word tells the reader how the two ideas connect.

cards.title: Two independent clauses
cards.body: A compound sentence joins two (or more) independent clauses: each could be a sentence on its own. Join them with a comma + a FANBOYS word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or with a semicolon.

cards.title: Pick the joining word that fits
cards.text:
and = adds: My brother plays guitar, and my sister sings.
but / yet = contrast: The test was hard, but I passed.
so = result: I was hungry, so I made a sandwich.
or = choice: You can take the bus, or you can walk.
; = closely linked: The bell rang; everyone cheered.
cards.note: The comma goes before the FANBOYS word, not after it.

cards.title: Compound sentence or compound predicate?
cards.telling: The dog barked and ran away.
cards.showing: The dog barked, and the cat ran away.
cards.note: Look after the joining word. Is there a new subject (the cat)? Then it’s a second clause, and it needs the comma.
